lesson.title: Inseparable Prefixes (ver-, be-, er-)
lesson.subtitle: ver- is English for-: vergessen = forget, verlieren = lose, verboten = forbidden

hook.title: The Bound Prefixes
hook.content: Some prefixes never fly. ver-, be-, and er- are welded to their verbs: they take the stress together, never split, and never leave for the sentence end. And the oldest of them, ver-, has been hiding in English all along: it is for-. vergessen is forget — the same for- plus the same get. verlieren is lose — and English's forlorn is literally 'for-lost', the identical construction. verboten is forbidden. When a German verb starts with ver-, an English for- is usually dead ahead.

footnotes.title: The No-ge- Law, Second Verse
footnotes.content: Inseparable verbs skip ge- in the participle for the same acoustic reason as -ieren verbs: verstanden (not 'geverstanden'), besucht, erklärt. The prefix and the stress rule you learned in the No-ge- Club now cover a second whole verb family.

pattern.title: The ver- for- Ledger, and the be-/er- Workshop
pattern.content: The ver- ledger: vergessen ↔ forget, verlieren ↔ lose (forlorn), verstehen ↔ understand (stehen/stand!), verkaufen ↔ sell (kaufen is the twin of cheap — both from the Latin for 'innkeeper/tradesman'), versuchen ↔ to try. The be- workshop: bekommen means GET, not become — 'come by' something; be- converts meaning the way it does in English bespeak. The er- workshop: erklären is 'make clear' (klar ↔ clear — both borrowed from Latin clarus), erinnern is to remember ('inner-ize' a thing). Stress law: the prefix never takes the stress — verGESsen, beKOMmen, erKLÄren. That unstressed prefix is exactly why inseparables reject ge-, just like -ieren verbs.
pattern.linguist_note: bekommen vs become is the most famous false friend in the app's deck: both are be + come, but English drifted the compound toward 'turn into' while German kept 'come by/receive'. The Review Hub's false-friend deck covers it in full.

exercises.prompt: Match the ver- verbs with their for-/English twins. Then recall earlier vocabulary in the short phrases:
exercises.target_answer: vergessen, verlieren, verstehen, verkaufen, Wir müssen aufwachen, Wir können zurückkommen, Wir können anrufen, Wir müssen einkaufen, Wir können abfahren, Wir können bekommen
exercises.meaning: to forget; to lose; to understand; to sell; We must wake up; We can come back; We can call; We must shop; We can depart; We can receive
exercises.explanation: ver- is English for-: for-get, for-lorn (lost), for-bidden — and verstehen stands under it all, like understand.

exercises.prompt: Find the pair that needs another connection, not the shared one.
exercises.meaning: Recognize a familiar German word by choosing between earlier connection patterns.
exercises.explanation: Pepper, path and pound use P → PF. Better → besser uses T → SS.

exercises.prompt: Run the be- workshop: 'Ich _____ einen Kaffee' (to get/receive):
exercises.english_hint: be + come — but it means GET
exercises.meaning: Ich bekomme einen Kaffee = I am getting a coffee
exercises.explanation: bekommen = 'come by' → receive. Never 'become' — that is the trap the false-friend deck drills.

exercises.prompt: What archaic English adjective meaning 'abandoned / hopeless' preserves the old participle of 'verlieren'?
exercises.explanation: forlorn is for- + the same lose-root as verlieren: the identical prefix, the identical verb, fossilized in English.

exercises.idea: someone asked you to bring the thing, and you have to confess: you have forgotten it
cues: haben opens the Perfekt bracket: ich habe
Inseparable verbs never take ge-: vergessen closes the bracket, prefix welded on
exercises.explanation: Perfekt bracket with an inseparable verb: 'habe' opens, 'vergessen' closes — no ge- anywhere.

diagnosis.cue: ver- is welded on — vergessen, never 'gevergessen'. The no-ge- law: inseparables and -ieren verbs skip the prefix.

summary.outcome: Decode ver-, be-, er- verbs via their English for-/be- twins and form ge--free participles.
summary.takeaway: ver- = for- (vergessen/forget, verlieren/forlorn), be- and er- reshape meaning — and inseparables never take ge-.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Next: the ver ↔ for- cognate set — vergessen is forget, verboten is forbidden: twelve words, one prefix.

twist.prompt: Wait — you remember after all: negate it. I have forgotten it becomes I have NOT forgotten it.
twist.explanation: nicht lands before the participle — inside the Perfekt bracket, where the action dies. And vergessen keeps its ge-free, inseparable dignity.

verlieren.etymology_derivation: ver- (for-) + lieren from Proto-Germanic *leusaną — the same root as English lose; forlorn is 'utterly lost' (forleosan), the exact ver- construction. [wiktionary]

bekommen.etymology_derivation: be- (by/around) + kommen (come) — literally 'come by (something)'; English become is the same be + come with a different job. [wiktionary]

erinnern.etymology_derivation: er- (out/thorough) + innern (inner) — to 'internal-ize' a thing; built on inn(inner), the twin of English inner. [wiktionary]

erklären.etymology_derivation: er- (out) + klar (clear) — 'to make clear'; klar and clear are both medieval loans of Latin clarus. [wiktionary]

verstehen.etymology_derivation: Inseparable: ver- (for-) + stehen (stand). Past participle: verstanden (no ge-).

versuchen.context_translation: I am trying to find it.

cousine.etymology_derivation: From French cousine, Latin consobrina — shared Romance loan with English cousin. [wiktionary]

bauch.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *būkaz 'belly, body' — cognate with dialectal English bouk. [wiktionary]

schwein.context_phrase: Das Schwein lebt auf dem Bauernhof.
schwein.context_translation: The pig lives on the farm.
schwein.etymology_derivation: Proto-West Germanic *swīn — the twin of English swine. [wiktionary]

soße.etymology_derivation: Soße — borrowed from French sauce, from Latin salsa (salted), so both English sauce and German Soße carry the same Latin salt-word. [wiktionary]

kollege.context_phrase: Mein Kollege kommt morgen ins Büro.
kollege.context_translation: My colleague is coming to the office tomorrow.
kollege.etymology_derivation: From Latin collega, the same loan that gives English colleague. [wiktionary]

eule.context_translation: The owl sleeps during the day.
eule.etymology_derivation: From Middle High German iule, from Old High German ūwila, from Proto-West Germanic *uwwulā, glossed owl. English owl continues the same West Germanic word. [wiktionary]

name.etymology_derivation: From Old High German namo, Proto-West Germanic *namō, the exact twin of English name. [wiktionary]

nadel.context_phrase: Ich nähe mit Nadel und Faden.
nadel.context_translation: I sew with needle and thread.
nadel.etymology_derivation: From Proto-West Germanic *nāþlu, from the sew-root (PIE *(s)neh₁-); the page documents cognate English needle — the same sewing-word. [wiktionary]
